Digi Power X pairs owned power infrastructure with Supermicro GPUs to serve enterprise AI customers Proactive uses images sourced from Shutterstock

Digi Power X Inc (NASDAQ:DGXX, FRA:1NQ0, NEO:DGX) is using Super Micro Computer Inc (NASDAQ:SMCI) servers built around Nvidia's latest Blackwell chips to sell AI computing capacity to enterprise customers, according to a Supermicro case study.

The company owns and operates the infrastructure behind its NeoCloudz platform, from power generation and substations to Tier III data centers. NeoCloudz rents GPU capacity on dedicated bare-metal servers, with no virtualization layer and no sharing of hardware among customers. The servers can be hosted at a Digi Power X facility or installed at a customer's site.

Digi Power X deployed Supermicro systems with Nvidia B200 and B300 GPUs, liquid cooling and Supermicro management software, the case study highlighted.

Supermicro said it wanted hardware that could handle both large-scale AI training and real-time inference.

The company said its ownership of power assets, including substations and on-site generation, sets it apart from traditional cloud providers. It said GPU rental rates reflect its actual power costs rather than the margins charged by those providers. It also said liquid-cooled, high-density racks fit more computing into less floor space, which lowers the cost per GPU-hour passed on to customers. As a result, Digi Power X said, it can offer Blackwell compute at rates traditional providers can't match.

Scalability was another priority. Digi Power X said it aims to add capacity in weeks rather than years, without large upfront capital outlays at each stage of growth.

For orchestration and billing, the company integrated three Supermicro software products: SuperCloud Composer, SuperCloud Developer Experience and SuperCloud Director. They give customers visibility into their workloads and automated, metered billing.

The data center environment includes high-density GPU rack rows with per-cabinet power monitoring, hot-aisle containment, expansion-ready room layouts and rack-level environmental sensing.

"DigiPowerX was built on the conviction that the AI infrastructure market needed a fundamentally different model — one where the operator controls the full stack, from power to compute, and passes those structural advantages directly to customers," said Alec Amar, president of Digi Power X.

"Supermicro has been a critical partner in executing that vision, giving us access to the latest NVIDIA Blackwell hardware and the software tooling to manage it at scale. The result is a platform we are proud to be already running in production for enterprise AI customers today."

The platform is already running in production for enterprise customers, the case study said.

title: What Was HPE Telling You Before Its Stock Ran?

What Was HPE Telling You Before Its Stock Ran?

Image from Pixabay

Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) stock returned 187.1%, counting dividends, in the twelve months to October 13, 2026. On September 2, 2026, the company reported record quarterly revenue, orders, and backlog. Executives credited demand for traditional servers, AI systems and networking, along with higher prices for those servers. Did the company say anything about that demand, or those server prices, before October 2025?

HPE Praised AI Demand, Then Faulted Its Own Pricing

Executives addressed these trends twice, though only one instance sounded like good news at the time. During the December 5, 2024 call for fiscal Q4 2024, management noted that demand for AI systems remained strong. Revenue for that quarter reached a record $8.5 billion, up 15.1% from a year earlier.

Three months later, during the March 6, 2025 call for fiscal Q1 2025, executives identified servers as a problem. Management stated that HPE had priced its traditional servers without fully accounting for the value of its inventory, and that unusually high AI inventory had squeezed server margins further. Server operating margin stood at 8.1%, a figure management called well below expectations. The shares struggled after that report. Only in hindsight does this look like a sign, because server pricing is exactly what management would highlight eighteen months later.

Financial filings from HPE showed this same mix of rising sales and weaker margins. Revenue grew 18.5% from a year earlier in fiscal Q3 2025. Yet operating margin for that quarter fell to 4.7%, down from 7.8% a year earlier. The stock was already rising as well: it returned 74.7% in the six months before the twelve-month window began on October 10, 2025.

How Big Was HPE's Run Against The S&P 500?

The S&P 500 returned about 18% over the same twelve months. That means HPE returned roughly ten times as much as the broader index. Almost all of that gain materialized in the last six months, when the stock returned 183%. HPE was not alone in this trend: Dell Technologies, one of its peers, did even better at 285.0%. Not every peer joined in, though, as IBM fell 14.8%.

The shift linking back to those earlier earnings calls occurred in servers, HPE's largest business at 52% of fiscal 2025 revenue. Server revenue rose 35% to an all-time high in fiscal Q3 2026. Executives noted that higher average selling prices for traditional servers made up for supply limits on how many units HPE could ship. This trajectory looks like the March 2025 pricing problem reversed.

title: What Changed For HPE Stock, And What Did Not?

Image from Pixabay

Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) stock returned 193.4% in the year to October 12, 2026, far outpacing the 20.5% return for the S&P 500. The company's sales growth sped up over those twelve months, and management raised its outlook for fiscal 2026 and fiscal 2027 on September 2, 2026. On September 30, it raised its long-term growth forecast for its networking business and announced a $1.2 billion AI order from cloud firm Vultr. So how much has the business itself grown over that year?

How Quickly Is HPE's Revenue Rising?

Sales over the last twelve months reached $41.9 billion, up 26.6% from $33.1 billion a year earlier. Revenue in fiscal Q3 2026 reached a record $12.2 billion. That figure was up 34% from a year earlier, management noted during the September 2, 2026 call. Just three quarters before that, sales were growing 14.4%. Unlike the order figure below, these growth rates are not adjusted for the acquired Juniper Networks.

Server revenue grew 35% in fiscal Q3 2026. Management stated that higher selling prices on traditional servers drove the increase, while supply limits restricted the total number of servers HPE could ship. AI systems brought in almost $1.6 billion of that quarter's sales.

What Does HPE Stock Cost Against Its Sales Now?

HPE stock currently costs 2.2 times the company's sales over the last twelve months. That multiple had stayed between 0.4 and 1.4 over the past ten years. The share price rose far faster than sales did, so buyers now pay more for each dollar of HPE's revenue than they did in any of those years. On earnings, the stock is priced at 33.7 times.

The stock price appears to assume sales will keep growing, and management is forecasting exactly that. The company expects fiscal Q4 2026 revenue of $13.9 billion to $14.8 billion, which is above the record it reported for Q3. Management now expects revenue to grow 13% to 17% for fiscal 2027. Orders grew 42% in fiscal Q3 2026, calculated on a basis that counts the acquired Juniper Networks in both years. Furthermore, HPE ended the quarter with a record backlog.

HPE's Margin Is Back At 7.8%

HPE kept 7.8% of its sales as operating profit over the last twelve months. This matches the 7.8% it kept two years ago. The margin fell to 6.2% a year ago and has since recovered, yet it remains below the 8.8% recorded three years ago. It is also far below the 18.5% posted by the S&P 500.

Management stated on the September 2, 2026 call that it expects its adjusted operating margin, which runs well above the 7.8% figure, to decline from the previous quarter. The company named a larger share of AI systems in what it sells among the reasons for this expected drop. The adjusted operating margin is the number to watch when the company reports fiscal Q4 2026.

Super Micro Computer (SMCI) has been one of the most searched-for stocks on Zacks.com lately. So, you might want to look at some of the facts that could shape the stock's performance in the near term.

Over the past month, shares of this server technology company have returned +8.8%, compared to the Zacks S&P 500 composite's +2.1% change. During this period, the Zacks Computer- Storage Devices industry, which Super Micro falls in, has lost 10.7%. The key question now is: What could be the stock's future direction?

While media releases or rumors about a substantial change in a company's business prospects usually make its stock 'trending' and lead to an immediate price change, there are always some fundamental facts that eventually dominate the buy-and-hold decision-making.

Earnings Estimate Revisions

Here at Zacks, we prioritize appraising the change in the projection of a company's future earnings over anything else. That's because we believe the present value of its future stream of earnings is what determines the fair value for its stock.

We essentially look at how sell-side analysts covering the stock are revising their earnings estimates to reflect the impact of the latest business trends. And if earnings estimates go up for a company, the fair value for its stock goes up. A higher fair value than the current market price drives investors' interest in buying the stock, leading to its price moving higher. This is why empirical research shows a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and near-term stock price movements.

For the current quarter, Super Micro is expected to post earnings of $1.06 per share, indicating a change of +202.9% from the year-ago quarter. The Zacks Consensus Estimate has changed -1.1% over the last 30 days.

For the current fiscal year, the consensus earnings estimate of $4.37 points to a change of +20.4% from the prior year. Over the last 30 days, this estimate has remained unchanged.

For the next fiscal year, the consensus earnings estimate of $5.13 indicates a change of +17.5% from what Super Micro is expected to report a year ago. Over the past month, the estimate has remained unchanged.

With an impressive externally audited track record, our proprietary stock rating tool -- the Zacks Rank -- is a more conclusive indicator of a stock's near-term price performance, as it effectively harnesses the power of earnings estimate revisions. The size of the recent change in the consensus estimate, along with three other factors related to earnings estimates, has resulted in a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold) for Super Micro.
